instruction: Study the Apurinã verb forms and their English translations. Deduce the morphological rules, then translate the English phrases by composing morpheme tiles.
taskFrame: Figure out how Apurinã builds its verbs. Then prove it.

verdicts.perfect: You speak a little Apurinã now.
verdicts.good: Almost there — Apurinã is starting to click.
verdicts.partial: Tricky language. The rainforest keeps its secrets.

queries.hintOnFail: Look at row 4 — it's the exact same phrase. This one is free!
queries.flavor: You're hungry after a long walk along the Purus River.

queries.hintOnFail: You need the 'we' prefix. Have you revealed all the context rows?
queries.flavor: Everyone sits down together for the meal.

queries.hintOnFail: The 'speak' root only appears in the gated rows 7-9.
queries.flavor: Your companion is telling a story by the fire.

queries.hintOnFail: Combine what you learned about 'we' with the 'speak' root.

hints.text: Compare rows 1-3: what stays the same, what changes? The changing part encodes person.
kaa- marks 'we (inclusive)'. It appears only in row 10 — you may need to reveal it.
Structure: [person prefix] + [verb root] + [aspect suffix]. Roots: pita=go, kuta=eat, nykata=speak. The suffix -ka marks progressive ('am doing'). Every answer can be assembled from this evidence.

lore.etymology: The name 'Apurinã' comes from the Apurinã people's self-designation. In their own language, they call themselves 'Popũkare' — the word 'Apurinã' was given by neighbouring groups and adopted by Portuguese colonists.
lore.geography: Spoken along the middle and upper Purus River in Amazonas state, Brazil — one of the Amazon's major southern tributaries. The Purus meanders through dense várzea floodplain forest, and Apurinã communities are scattered across a 600km stretch.
lore.speakers: Approximately 2,800–3,600 speakers remain (2023 estimates). The language is losing ground to Portuguese among younger generations in communities closer to urban centres like Lábrea and Tapauá.
lore.family: Arawakan — one of the largest language families in South America, stretching from the Caribbean (Taíno, Garifuna) through Central Amazonia. Apurinã is part of the Purus branch, relatively distant from the better-known Arawakan languages of the northern Amazon.
lore.culturalNote: The Apurinã are known for their intricate ritual knowledge tied to the xingané ceremony — a multi-day celebration involving elaborate body painting with genipapo dye, ritual combat, and the consumption of fermented drinks. The verb morphology you just decoded encodes tense, aspect, and person in a single word — a hallmark of polysynthetic Amazonian languages.
lore.endangerment: Classified as 'Severely Endangered' by UNESCO. Active documentation projects exist (notably by Sidney da Silva Facundes at UFPA), but intergenerational transmission is declining.
lore.funFact: Apurinã has a complex system of evidentiality — speakers grammatically mark whether they witnessed an event, heard about it, or inferred it. You can't say 'it rained' without revealing whether you saw the rain yourself.
lore.briefingHook: A language where you cannot describe an event without revealing how you know it happened.
lore.lineageNote: Related to Taíno — the first indigenous language Columbus encountered in the Caribbean. Same family, 4,000 km apart.

taskFrame: Swahili packs who and when into a single word. Unpack it.

verdicts.perfect: Hongera — you conjugate like a Nairobi local.
verdicts.good: Karibu — almost there. The prefixes are settling in.
verdicts.partial: Swahili rewards patience. The pattern is in there.

queries.hintOnFail: Every piece is on the board: 'I' from rows 1 and 4, 'will' from rows 6 and 7, 'like' from rows 1 and 4.
queries.flavor: Tomorrow, you finally tell them.

queries.hintOnFail: 'They' appears only in row 7 — but there with 'will'. Borrow the prefix, swap the tense.
queries.flavor: The students open their books.

queries.hintOnFail: 'Sing' only shows up with 'they' and 'he'. It transfers — combine tu + past + imba.
queries.flavor: Last night, around the fire, everyone joined in.

hints.text: Compare rows 1 and 4 — same person, different time. The middle piece carries the tense.
'ta' puts the action in the future.
Structure: [who] + [when] + [verb]. ni=I, u=you, a=he/she, tu=we, wa=they · na=present, li=past, ta=future.

lore.etymology: 'Swahili' comes from Arabic sawāḥil, 'coasts' — the language grew up on the East African shore where Bantu speakers traded with Arab and Persian merchants.
lore.geography: East Africa: a national language in Tanzania and Kenya, with speakers across Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, Mozambique and the DRC. Zanzibar's Stone Town is its historic heart.
lore.speakers: Over 80 million speakers, most using it as a second language — the most widely spoken language in Africa, and still growing.
lore.family: Niger-Congo, Bantu branch — the vast family covering most of sub-Saharan Africa. Swahili is Bantu grammar wearing centuries of Arabic, Persian, and Portuguese loanwords from the coastal trade.
lore.culturalNote: Swahili time starts at sunrise: 7 AM is 'saa moja', hour one of the day. The tense markers you just used (-na-, -li-, -ta-) sit inside the verb, so a single word carries a whole sentence.
lore.endangerment: Not endangered — vigorous and expanding. It's an official language of the African Union, and the UN marks World Kiswahili Language Day every July 7.
lore.funFact: 'Hakuna matata' is real Swahili — 'there are no problems'. Simba (lion), rafiki (friend), and jambo (hello) all traveled the world through film.
lore.briefingHook: The language that gave the world 'hakuna matata' — where one word holds who, when, and what.
lore.lineageNote: Its verb machinery is cousin to Zulu and Xhosa; its dictionary carries a thousand years of monsoon trade with Arabia, Persia, and India.

title: Vowel Harmony
instruction: Study the Turkish nouns and their plurals. Find the rule that picks the plural ending, then compose the translations from morpheme tiles.
taskFrame: One rule runs Turkish: vowels must agree. Find it, and every plural is yours.

verdicts.good: Çok iyi — nearly singing in tune.
verdicts.partial: Turkish is a song; you caught a few notes.

queries.hintOnFail: 'Eye' is row 4. Its vowel is a front vowel, like in 'el' (row 9) — pick the matching ending.
queries.flavor: The watchtower keeps two of them on the horizon.

queries.hintOnFail: The dotless ı is a back vowel — it behaves like the a in 'atlar'.
queries.flavor: The children race each other home from school.

queries.hintOnFail: ü looks exotic but it's a front vowel — same family as the e in 'evler'.
queries.flavor: The harvest festival lasts a whole week.

hints.text: Say rows 7 and 8 out loud. Look only at the last vowel of each root.
The plural ending has two costumes: -lar or -ler.
Vowel harmony: the ending copies the root's last vowel family. Back vowels (a, ı, o, u) → -lar. Front vowels (e, i, ö, ü) → -ler.

lore.etymology: 'Türk' may trace to an old root for 'strength' or 'ripeness'. The language renamed itself when the Republic did — since the 1930s it has called itself Türkçe.
lore.geography: Türkiye, Cyprus, and the Balkans, with large communities in Germany — and echoing cousins in a great arc across Central Asia.
lore.speakers: Around 80–90 million native speakers — by far the largest Turkic language.
lore.family: Turkic — close cousins with Azerbaijani and Turkmen, more distant with Uzbek, Kazakh, and Uyghur, stretching from the Mediterranean to Siberia.
lore.culturalNote: Vowel harmony is not just grammar, it's music: every suffix echoes the root's last vowel, so words 'sing in tune'. In 1928 the country swapped the Arabic script for Latin letters in a matter of months — one of history's fastest writing reforms.
lore.endangerment: Not endangered — the official language of Türkiye, with a thriving press, literature, and music scene.
lore.funFact: Turkish stacks endings into famously long words — 'muvaffakiyetsizleştiricileştiriveremeyebileceklerimizdenmişsinizcesine' means roughly 'as if you were one of those we could not easily turn into a maker of unsuccessful people.'
lore.briefingHook: A language where vowels must hold hands — and the whole grammar follows their lead.
lore.lineageNote: Its vowel harmony so charmed linguists that they once proposed a grand 'Altaic' family linking Turkish to Mongolian — maybe even Korean and Japanese.

taskFrame: Quechua verbs wear their subject at the end. Decode the endings.

verdicts.good: Almost — the Andes are steep, but you're climbing.
verdicts.partial: Even the Inca road was built one stone at a time.

queries.hintOnFail: Row 6 has 'walk'; rows 1 and 4 have 'I'. Snap them together.
queries.flavor: The trail over the pass begins before dawn.

queries.hintOnFail: 'We' only appears in rows 7 and 8 — a long ending that includes the listener.
queries.flavor: From the summit, everyone looks out over the Sacred Valley.

queries.hintOnFail: Careful: 'she' and 'I' differ by a single vowel — compare rows 3 and 4.
queries.flavor: Lunch is quinoa soup — she's already at the table.

hints.text: Rows 1–3 share a root. Watch the ending change with the person.
'nchik' means we — including the person you're talking to.
Structure: [root] + [person]. ni=I, nki=you, n=he/she, nchik=we (incl.). Watch out: -n and -ni differ by one vowel.

lore.etymology: Speakers call it Runasimi — 'the people's speech'. 'Quechua' may come from qheswa, the name for the temperate valleys where it spread.
lore.geography: The Andes of Peru, Bolivia, and Ecuador, spilling into Colombia, Argentina, and Chile — the spine of South America, from sea level to 5,000 metres.
lore.speakers: Roughly 7–8 million speakers — the most widely spoken indigenous language family of the Americas.
lore.family: Quechuan — really a family of related varieties rather than one language. The Cuzco variety in this puzzle descends from the administrative language of the Inca Empire.
lore.culturalNote: The Inca ran an empire of millions without writing, using knotted khipu cords — and this language. The inclusive 'we' you just used (-nchik) grammatically insists the listener belongs: a worldview baked into the verb.
lore.endangerment: UNESCO lists several Quechua varieties as vulnerable under Spanish pressure, but radio, music, and bilingual school programs are pushing back.
lore.funFact: You already speak some Quechua: llama, puma, condor, quinoa, coca, and jerky (from ch'arki) all hitchhiked into English from the Andes.
lore.briefingHook: The empire's language with no way to leave the listener out of 'we'.
lore.lineageNote: Its neighbour Aymara is famous among linguists for picturing the future as behind you — unseen — and the past as stretched out in front.

title: Both Ends of the Verb
instruction: Study the Classical Nahuatl verb forms and their English translations. The verb marks its subject at the front and 'many' at the back — then compose the translations from morpheme tiles.
taskFrame: Nahuatl marks who at the front and how many at the back. Handle both ends.

verdicts.perfect: Qualli — both ends of the verb answer to you.
verdicts.good: So close — the Aztec scribes would nod.
verdicts.partial: The codices took years to read. You're faster.

queries.hintOnFail: Rows 1 and 4 start with 'I'; row 5 ends with 'sing'.
queries.flavor: The dawn ceremony needs your voice.

queries.hintOnFail: 'They' needs no prefix — just the plural tail from row 6.
queries.flavor: The children miss their grandmother's stories.

queries.hintOnFail: 'We' is both ends at once: the 'I' prefix plus the plural tail. Row 7 shows it with 'sleep'.
queries.flavor: The whole plaza sings together.

hints.text: Rows 1 and 7 are both 'I sleep'… except one is plural. What got added, and where?
A lone 'h' at the end makes the subject plural.
Structure: [who] + [verb] + (h if plural). ni=I/we, ti=you, nothing=he/she/they. 'We' = ni- plus -h: both ends at once.

lore.etymology: 'Nāhuatl' likely comes from a root meaning 'clear, audible speech' — the language that sounds like it means it.
lore.geography: Central Mexico: Puebla, Guerrero, Veracruz, Hidalgo, and the valleys around Mexico City — the old Aztec heartland.
lore.speakers: About 1.7 million speakers today — Mexico's largest indigenous language, though many local varieties are losing young speakers to Spanish.
lore.family: Uto-Aztecan — a family stretching from the US Great Basin (Shoshone, Ute, Comanche) down to El Salvador (Pipil). Hopi is a distant cousin.
lore.culturalNote: Classical Nahuatl was the language of Aztec law, astronomy, and poetry. Its poetry built meaning from paired metaphors: 'flower and song' meant poetry itself; 'water and mountain' meant a city.
lore.endangerment: Many varieties are endangered, but revitalization is real: Nahuatl hip-hop, TikTok teachers, and university chairs keep the language audible.
lore.funFact: You speak Nahuatl every day: chocolate (xocolātl), tomato (tomatl), avocado (āhuacatl), chili (chīlli), coyote (coyōtl), ocelot (ocēlōtl).
lore.briefingHook: The empire's language hiding in your kitchen: chocolate, tomato, avocado, coyote.
lore.lineageNote: Cousin to Hopi and Shoshone — its quiet plural -h is an echo of sound-changes that once swept half the American West.

taskFrame: Figure out how Esperanto marks time. Then prove it.

verdicts.good: Almost fluent — the endings are clicking.
verdicts.partial: Tricky, but the pattern is perfectly regular. Look again.

li + manĝ + past ending. Every piece is in the evidence.

hints.text: Rows 1-3 differ only at the end. The ending carries the tense.
-is marks the past. Every past form in the evidence ends in -is.
Structure: [pronoun] + [root] + [tense]. -as = present, -is = past, -os = future. mi=I, vi=you, li=he, ni=we, ili=they.

lore.etymology: 'Esperanto' means 'one who hopes' — the pen name of L. L. Zamenhof, who published the language in Warsaw in 1887.
lore.geography: Spoken worldwide: congresses, clubs, and a native-speaking community of children raised in Esperanto households.
lore.speakers: Estimates range from 100,000 to 2 million; around 1,000 native speakers. Duolingo's Esperanto course has millions of learners.
lore.family: Constructed, with Romance and Germanic vocabulary and a Slavic-inspired structure. Designed for regularity: 16 rules, no exceptions.
lore.culturalNote: Esperanto was meant to be a neutral second language for peace. Its congresses still run entirely in Esperanto — a century-old experiment that never quite died.
lore.endangerment: Not endangered in the usual sense — but its native-speaker community is tiny and precious to linguists.
lore.funFact: Every Esperanto verb ending is fixed: -as is always present, -is always past, -os always future. No irregular verbs exist. At all.
lore.briefingHook: A language with zero irregular verbs. The puzzle practically solves itself — if you trust the pattern.
lore.lineageNote: Its vocabulary cousin is French and Latin; its idealism cousin is the internet itself.

taskFrame: Figure out how Indonesian makes things plural. Then prove it.

verdicts.perfect: Bagus sekali! You pluralize like a Jakartan.
verdicts.good: Almost there — the doubling trick is clicking.
verdicts.partial: The pattern is hiding in plain sight. Say the words out loud.

queries.hintOnFail: Row 5 is the exact same phrase. This one is free!
Compare rows 1-2: the plural just says the word twice.
Same doubling trick as rows 2 and 4.
The 'book' root is in gated row 7 — reveal it, then double it.
'We' is kami from gated row 9. The verb never changes.
queries.flavor: The whole family sits down together.

hints.text: Rows 1-2 and 3-4: what happens to the word when the meaning becomes plural?
Reduplication: saying the word twice makes it plural. anak-anak = children.
Plural = full reduplication (word-word). Verbs never change: saya=I, mereka=they, kami=we, makan=eat.

lore.etymology: 'Indonesia' means 'Indian islands' in Greek — a name adopted at independence in 1945.
lore.geography: The world's fourth most populous nation: 17,000 islands from Sumatra to Papua. Jakarta is the capital.
lore.speakers: Over 270 million people use Indonesian; ~43 million speak it natively. It is one of the fastest-growing languages on earth.
lore.family: Austronesian — the great seafaring family stretching from Madagascar to Easter Island. Malay is its closest kin.
lore.culturalNote: Indonesian was chosen at independence precisely because it belonged to no single ethnic group — a trade tongue promoted into a national language in one generation.
lore.endangerment: Thriving — though its success pressures hundreds of smaller regional languages like Javanese and Sundanese.
lore.funFact: Plurals by repetition: anak-anak (children), kuda-kuda (horses). In casual speech you can even drop the repetition if context is clear.
lore.briefingHook: A language where the plural is just saying the word twice.
lore.lineageNote: Cousin to Hawaiian, Māori, and Malagasy — one family that sailed half the planet.

title: Harmony Endings
instruction: Study the Finnish words and their English translations. Deduce the plural and the 'in the…' endings — including which vowel goes with which word — then translate by composing tiles.
taskFrame: Figure out how Finnish endings harmonize with their roots. Then prove it.

verdicts.perfect: Täydellistä! Even the vowels obey you.
verdicts.good: Almost — the harmony rule is starting to ring true.
verdicts.partial: Listen to the vowels. Front words want front endings.

queries.hintOnFail: Row 2 is the exact same word. This one is free!
Row 3 shows it: back-vowel roots take -ssa.
Plural -t works for every root. Row 5 proves it.
kylä has front vowels (ä) — so it takes the front ending -ssä, not -ssa. Row 6.
queries.flavor: The front vowels demand their own ending.

queries.hintOnFail: koulu has back vowels (o, u) — back ending -ssa. Gated row 9 confirms it.

hints.text: Rows 3 and 6 both mean 'in the…' but the endings differ. What differs about the roots?
-ssä is the front-vowel twin of -ssa. kylä (with ä) takes -ssä.
Plural is always -t. 'In the' is -ssa after back vowels (a, o, u) and -ssä after front vowels (ä, ö, y). The vowels must harmonize.

lore.etymology: 'Suomi' — the Finns' own name for their country — has no certain origin. Outsiders' 'Finland' likely comes from an old Germanic word for wanderers.
lore.geography: Finland: lakes, forests, and the Arctic north. Helsinki sits on the Gulf of Finland, a short ferry from Estonia.
lore.speakers: About 5.5 million speakers — nearly all in Finland, with communities in Sweden and Norway.
lore.family: Uralic — kin to Estonian and Hungarian, and famously unrelated to Swedish or Russian despite the neighbours.
lore.culturalNote: Finnish holds the world record for the longest palindromic word (saippuakivikauppias: travelling soapstone salesman) and compulsory vowel harmony that singers feel in their mouths.
lore.endangerment: Safe and thriving — though small dialects like Ingrian face extinction.
lore.funFact: Finnish vowels come in front and back teams that refuse to mix: talo takes -ssa, kylä demands -ssä. The mouth position must match.
lore.briefingHook: A language where the vowels vote — and the ending must obey the majority.
lore.lineageNote: Distant cousin to Hungarian — though a Finn and a Hungarian can't understand a word of each other's speech.

title: Who Is 'We'?
instruction: Study the Māori pronouns and their English translations. Deduce how 'we' changes with who is included — then translate by composing tiles.
taskFrame: Figure out how Māori draws the line around 'we'. Then prove it.

verdicts.perfect: Ka mau te wehi! You know exactly who 'we' is.
verdicts.good: Almost — the inclusive/exclusive line is getting clearer.
verdicts.partial: The secret is who counts as 'we'. Compare rows 4 and 5.

queries.hintOnFail: Row 4 is the exact same word. This one is free!
tā- includes the listener (row 5), -tou means more than two (row 6). Gated row 7 confirms it.
rā- marks 'they' (gated rows 8-9), -ua marks exactly two (rows 4-5).
Combine rā- (they) with -tou (plural). Row 9.
mā- excludes the listener (row 4), -tou is plural. Row 6.
queries.flavor: Talking about your own group to an outsider.

hints.text: Rows 4 and 5 share an ending but mean different 'we's. The first half decides who is included.
tā- includes the person you're talking to; mā- excludes them. -ua = two people, -tou = more.
[who] + [how many]: mā- = we-not-you, tā- = we-incl-you, rā- = they; -ua = two, -tou = three or more.

lore.etymology: 'Māori' means 'ordinary, normal' — the ordinary people, as opposed to spirits or strangers.
lore.geography: Aotearoa (New Zealand): from the subtropical north to the Southern Alps. Wellington is the capital.
lore.speakers: Around 200,000 speakers; an official language since 1987. Kōhanga reo (language nests) revived it from steep decline.
lore.family: Polynesian — close kin to Hawaiian, Samoan, and Tahitian. Its great voyages settled a triangle spanning a third of the globe.
lore.culturalNote: The haka, the hongi greeting, and whakapapa genealogies that recite dozens of generations — Māori draws identity from exactly who counts as 'us', which is what this puzzle is about.
lore.endangerment: Revitalizing: UNESCO lists it as vulnerable, but immersion schools and official status have reversed the decline.
lore.funFact: Māori has four kinds of 'we': you-and-I, us-two-not-you, all-of-us-incl-you, us-not-you. English makes do with one.
lore.briefingHook: A language with four different words for 'we' — because who is included matters.
lore.lineageNote: Sister to Hawaiian — the two split only ~800 years ago, when canoes carried Polynesians to Aotearoa.

verdicts.good: Almost — the class prefixes are falling into place.
verdicts.partial: Group the words by meaning, then watch the prefixes.

queries.hintOnFail: Row 3 is the exact same word. This one is free!
Take 'child' from row 1 and swap um- for the people-plural aba- from row 2.
Things take isi- in the singular (row 5). People take um-.
Row 6: the thing-plural is izi-.
The 'student' root only appears in gated row 7. Students are people — people-plural aba-.

hints.text: Rows 1-4 are people, rows 5-6 are things. Do the prefixes care?
aba- is the plural for people (class 2). izi- is the plural for things (class 8).
People: um- (one) → aba- (many). Things: isi- (one) → izi- (many). Pick the prefix by class AND number.

lore.etymology: 'Zulu' comes from the legendary founder Zulu kaMalandela — the name means 'heaven' or 'sky'.
lore.geography: KwaZulu-Natal province, South Africa: Indian Ocean coast rising to the Drakensberg mountains. Durban is the great port city.
lore.speakers: Over 14 million speakers — South Africa's most-spoken home language, and an official language since 1994.
lore.family: Bantu — the giant subfamily that spread farming and iron across half of Africa. Xhosa and Swazi are its closest kin.
lore.culturalNote: Zulu is famous for its clicks (c, q, x) borrowed from Khoisan neighbours — and for a noun-class system where adjectives, verbs, and pronouns all agree with the noun's class.
lore.endangerment: Safe and growing — one of Africa's most vital languages.
lore.funFact: Zulu nouns come in classes like teams: people wear um-/aba-, things wear isi-/izi-. The prefix tells you what kind of thing you're talking about.
lore.briefingHook: A language where every noun wears its team's jersey — and the jersey changes in the plural.
lore.lineageNote: Close cousin to Swahili (already in your rotation) — same Bantu engine, different paint job. Compare their prefixes!
